e.etymology: Of uncertain origin. It may come from Ardath, a place name in the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras that Marie Corelli used as the title of an 1889 novel, reshaped on the model of Edith.
A respelling of Melissa, the Greek word for honeybee, from meli, 'honey'. In Greek myth Melissa was a nymph who cared for the infant Zeus.
An American name of the 1960s and 70s that puts the La- prefix on Tricia, the short form of Patricia (Latin patricius, 'noble').
A spelling of Jerry, the pet form of Geraldine for girls and of Gerald, Jerome and Jeremiah for boys. This spelling was used mostly for girls in the 1930s and 40s.
A spelling of Cathy, the short form of Catherine, from Greek Aikaterine. The name's first meaning is debated, but it has long been tied to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
From the Christian spring holiday, whose English name goes back to Old English Eastre. It was given to children born at Easter and was also an old spoken form of Esther.
A respelling of Candy, which is both a short form of Candace and the English word for sweets.
namesakes: Kandi Burruss (singer and Real Housewives of Atlanta star)

assoc.t: candy, the word for sweets (same sound)

e.etymology: A respelling of Brandy, from the English word for the spirit distilled from wine (Dutch brandewijn, 'burnt wine'). It caught on in the 1970s as a feminine match for Brandon.
A respelling of Shannon, from the River Shannon in Ireland. Its Irish name, Sionainn, is linked to Old Irish sen, 'old' or 'wise', and in legend to the goddess Sionann.
A respelling of Cheryl, a 20th-century English coinage that probably blends Cherie or Cherry with the ending of Beryl. Cherie comes from French chérie, 'darling'.
A spelling of Gerry, the pet form of Geraldine, the feminine of Gerald, from Germanic ger, 'spear', and wald, 'rule'.
A respelling of Caitlin, the Irish form of Catherine, which reached Ireland through Old French Cateline. Catherine has long been tied to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
A spelling of Ed, the short form of Edward, Edwin, Edgar and Edmund. All begin with Old English ead, 'wealth' or 'fortune'.

assoc.t: Edd, called Double D, in the cartoon Ed, Edd n Eddy

e.etymology: A Scandinavian name from Old Norse huldr, 'hidden', also tied to Swedish huld, 'gracious, dear'. A separate Hebrew name, Huldah, belongs to a prophetess in 2 Kings. Scandinavian immigrants brought it to the US.
A spelling of Keisha, an African American name from the 1960s that may go back to the biblical Keziah. Keshia Knight Pulliam, who played Rudy on The Cosby Show, lifted this spelling in the 1980s.
namesakes: Keshia Knight Pulliam (Rudy on The Cosby Show)

e.etymology: From Welsh glyn, 'valley', the same word behind Glenn. It is used as a first name and a surname.
A spelling of Tanisha, an African American name that spread in the 1970s after actress Ta-Tanisha appeared on the TV series Room 222. It fits the Ta- and -isha patterns of that era.
In the US, a 1970s name in the Sha- family, close to Shantae and Chanté. Shanta is separately an Indian name from Sanskrit shanta, 'calm, peaceful'.
An American elaboration of Donna, Italian for 'lady', with the Spanish diminutive ending -ita. It also served as a feminine form of Don.
A respelling of Candace, the Greek form of kandake, the title of the queens of ancient Kush (Nubia). One of them is mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.
A spelling of Trina, the short form of Katrina, a form of Catherine. Catherine has long been tied to Greek katharos, 'pure'.
A variant of Alberta, the feminine of Albert, from Germanic adal, 'noble', and beraht, 'bright'. This spelling follows Bertha.
A spelling of Latonya, an African American name of the 1970s that joins the La- prefix to Tonya or Tonia, short forms of Antonia.
An African American name that peaked around 1990, built from the Sha- prefix and the -niqua ending shared with Taniqua and Moniqua.
e.note: Has often been used in jokes and memes as a stereotyped Black woman's name.

e.etymology: An African American name of the 1970s and 80s, built from the Sha- prefix and the ending of Tamika.
A spelling of Sherry or Sheri, names that grew out of French chérie, 'darling', with some help from sherry, the Spanish wine.
A spelling of Tonya, short for Antonia or its Russian relative Antonina, both from the Roman family name Antonius. The Taw- spelling echoes Tawny.
A respelling of Christine, the French form of Christina, from Latin Christianus, 'follower of Christ'. Christ comes from Greek christos, 'anointed'.
The pen name of English novelist Maria Louise Ramé (1839-1908), taken from her own childhood attempt to say Louise. Her bestsellers carried the name to the American South.
A spelling of Imogene, from Imogen, the heroine of Shakespeare's Cymbeline. Imogen is thought to be a misprint of Innogen, a legendary British name linked to Gaelic inghean, 'maiden'.
An elaboration of Shirley with the -ene ending. Shirley is an English place name and surname from Old English scir, 'bright', and leah, 'clearing'.
A shortened form of Teresa, a name first recorded in Spain and often linked to Greek therizo, 'to harvest', or the island of Thera.
